bone-forming tumours.md:
## 1. Overview and general principles
- **Bone-forming (osteogenic) tumours** are defined by tumour cells that **produce osteoid or bone directly**.
- **WHO 2020 classification of osteogenic tumours:**
  - **Benign:** osteoma, osteoid osteoma.
  - **Intermediate (locally aggressive):** osteoblastoma.
  - **Malignant:** osteosarcoma and its subtypes (conventional, telangiectatic, small cell, low-grade central, parosteal, periosteal, high-grade surface, secondary).
- **Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour** (excluding myeloma, which is a marrow neoplasm). Chondrosarcoma is second, Ewing sarcoma third (second in children).
- **Clinical age clue:** under 5 years, a destructive bone lesion is usually metastatic neuroblastoma or LCH; 10-25 years osteosarcoma or Ewing; over 40 years metastasis or myeloma first, then chondrosarcoma.
- **Investigation sequence for a suspicious lesion:** plain radiographs in two planes, **MRI of the whole bone** (extent, soft tissue mass, skip lesions, neurovascular relations), **CT chest** (lung metastases), bone scan or **PET-CT** (bone metastases), then **biopsy last**, at the treating sarcoma centre.
- **Biopsy rules (Mankin):** core needle preferred; tract **in line with the definitive incision** so it can be excised en bloc; go **through a single muscle compartment**, not between intermuscular planes; avoid neurovascular bundles and joints; meticulous haemostasis; drains brought out in line with the incision. Mankin showed that biopsies done outside specialist centres caused significantly more errors and changes in treatment, including unnecessary amputation.

### Surgical margins (Enneking)
| Margin | Plane of dissection | Result for high-grade sarcoma |
|---|---|---|
| **Intralesional** | Through the tumour | Gross residual tumour; nearly always recurs |
| **Marginal** | Through the reactive zone (pseudocapsule) | Leaves satellite lesions; high recurrence |
| **Wide** | Through normal tissue with a cuff around the reactive zone | Standard goal for limb salvage |
| **Radical** | Entire anatomical compartment removed | Rarely needed now with chemotherapy |

### Enneking (MSTS) staging
| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Benign 1 (latent)** | Inactive, well-marginated, often heals spontaneously (e.g. NOF) |
| **Benign 2 (active)** | Growing, contained within bone (e.g. most osteoid osteomas) |
| **Benign 3 (aggressive)** | Breaches cortex, may metastasise rarely (e.g. osteoblastoma, GCT) |
| **IA / IB** | Low grade, intracompartmental (A) or extracompartmental (B) |
| **IIA / IIB** | High grade, intra- or extracompartmental. **Most osteosarcomas are IIB** |
| **III** | Any grade with distant metastases |

- **AJCC 8th edition (appendicular skeleton):** T1 is 8 cm or less, T2 over 8 cm, T3 discontinuous tumours (skip lesions) in the primary bone; M1a lung only, M1b other distant sites. Stage IV = metastatic (IVA lung only; IVB other sites or nodes).

## 2. Osteoma and bone island
- **Osteoma:** dense lamellar bone on the surface of the **skull, facial bones and paranasal sinuses** (frontal sinus commonest). Usually asymptomatic.
- **Gardner syndrome:** multiple osteomas + **familial adenomatous polyposis** (APC gene, chromosome 5q) + desmoid tumours and epidermoid cysts. Colonic polyps have near 100% malignant potential, so osteomas of the jaw should prompt colonoscopy.
- **Bone island (enostosis):** intramedullary compact bone; **"thorny" radiating spicules (brush border)** blending into surrounding trabeculae; commonly pelvis and proximal femur.
  - Usually cold or mildly warm on bone scan, which helps distinguish it from **osteoblastic metastasis** (hot).
  - Over 2 cm = **giant bone island**. Growth over time warrants biopsy only if behaviour is atypical.
- **Osteopoikilosis:** multiple bone islands around joints (LEMD3 gene), asymptomatic; **Buschke-Ollendorff** when combined with skin lesions.

## 3. Osteoid osteoma
### Epidemiology and pathology
- About 10-12% of benign bone tumours. **Age 5-25 years**; **male to female about 2-3:1**.
- **Sites:** **proximal femur (femoral neck and intertrochanteric region) is the commonest**, then tibia; about 10% in the spine (**posterior elements**, lumbar commonest); hand and foot.
- **Nidus under 1.5 cm** (some texts 2 cm): interlacing osteoid trabeculae lined by osteoblasts in vascular fibrous stroma, surrounded by **reactive sclerosis**. Not malignant; no malignant transformation.
- Pain mediated by **prostaglandin E2 and COX-2** production in the nidus; the nidus contains **unmyelinated nerve fibres**.
- **FOS gene rearrangements** are now recognised in both osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma.

### Clinical features
- **Night pain relieved dramatically by aspirin or NSAIDs** (classic; about 75%).
- **Spine:** **painful scoliosis** (stiff, non-structural), the **lesion is on the concave side at the apex** of the curve; paravertebral spasm. Early removal (within about 15 months) allows the curve to resolve.
- **Intra-articular (hip, elbow, ankle):** synovitis, effusion, stiffness, little sclerosis; mimics inflammatory arthritis or infection; delayed diagnosis common.
- **Near the physis in children:** overgrowth and limb length discrepancy; muscle wasting.

### Imaging
- **Radiograph:** small **radiolucent nidus with dense surrounding sclerosis** and cortical thickening (cortical type commonest); the nidus may be hidden by sclerosis.
- **CT (thin slices) is the investigation of choice to locate the nidus**; nidus may show central mineralisation (target).
- **Bone scan:** intense uptake, **"double-density sign"** (hot nidus within a less hot reactive zone).
- **MRI:** marked marrow and soft tissue oedema may mislead (mimics infection or tumour); dynamic contrast shows early arterial enhancement of the nidus.

### Differential diagnosis
- **Brodie abscess** (serpiginous lucent tract, often crosses physis, no nidus calcification), **stress fracture** (linear lucency perpendicular to cortex), osteoblastoma (larger), chronic osteomyelitis, intracortical haemangioma.

### Management
| Option | Indication / notes |
|---|---|
| **NSAIDs** | Many lesions burn out in 2-4 years (natural history); acceptable if tolerated |
| **CT-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA)** | **Treatment of choice** for most accessible lesions; primary success about 90%, recurrence about 5-10%, can be repeated. Heats nidus to about 90 degrees C for 4-6 min |
| **Surgical excision (en bloc or burr-down)** | Lesion near skin (burn risk), near nerve roots or spinal cord (relative caution with RFA), failed RFA, need for histology |
| **Spine** | Excision or RFA with neural protection; early treatment to prevent structural scoliosis |

- Recurrence of pain after treatment means incomplete nidus removal.

> Exam pearl: Osteoid osteoma = nidus under 1.5 cm, night pain relieved by NSAIDs (PGE2/COX-2), proximal femur commonest, CT best to find the nidus, "double-density" on bone scan, painful scoliosis with the lesion on the CONCAVE side at the apex, RFA is the treatment of choice.

## 4. Osteoblastoma
- **Over 1.5-2 cm**, histologically similar to osteoid osteoma but **progressively growing** and **locally aggressive** (Enneking benign 3 in many cases).
- **Age 10-30**, male predominance.
- **Spine and sacrum are the commonest sites (about 40%)**, again in the **posterior elements**; also long bones (metadiaphysis) and talus.
- Dull ache, **less night pain and poor response to NSAIDs**; may cause **radiculopathy or cord compression**, and painful scoliosis.
- **Imaging:** expansile lytic lesion with variable mineralisation and a thin rim of reactive bone; **secondary ABC change** is common; soft tissue extension.
- **Differential:** **osteoblastoma-like osteosarcoma** (permeative margin, infiltration of host trabeculae), ABC, GCT.
- **Treatment:** **extended curettage with adjuvant (high-speed burr, phenol, cryotherapy) and grafting**, or **en bloc resection** for aggressive and spinal lesions (with stabilisation). Recurrence after curettage about 10-20%. Radiotherapy is avoided.
- **Epithelioid ("aggressive") osteoblastoma** has a higher recurrence risk.

## 5. Conventional osteosarcoma
### Epidemiology and risk factors
- **Bimodal:** peak in **adolescence (10-20 years, growth spurt)** and a second peak **over 60 years** (secondary: Paget disease, irradiation). Slight male predominance.
- **Sites:** metaphysis of long bones with the fastest growth: **distal femur > proximal tibia > proximal humerus** (about 50% around the knee). Axial (pelvis, spine) lesions in older patients carry a worse prognosis.
- **Genetic associations:**
  - **Hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1, chromosome 13q14)**: large increase in risk, also in irradiated fields.
  - **Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53, 17p13)**: osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumours, leukaemia, adrenocortical carcinoma.
  - **Rothmund-Thomson syndrome (RECQL4)**: poikiloderma, radial ray defects, osteosarcoma.
  - Werner (WRN) and Bloom (BLM) syndromes (RecQ helicases).
- **Secondary osteosarcoma:**
  - **Paget sarcoma:** in about 1% of Paget disease (higher in polyostotic disease); pelvis, femur, humerus; new pain or swelling in pagetic bone; **very poor prognosis** (5-year survival under 10-15%).
  - **Post-radiation sarcoma (Cahan criteria):** arises in the radiation field, latency of **over 3-4 years** (median about 10-15 years), histologically different from the original lesion. Osteosarcoma is the commonest radiation-induced bone sarcoma.
  - Others: fibrous dysplasia, bone infarct, chronic osteomyelitis (rare).

### Pathology
- **Diagnostic criterion: malignant spindle (pleomorphic) cells producing osteoid directly**. Amount of osteoid can be small.
- High grade; histological subtypes of conventional OS: **osteoblastic (commonest), chondroblastic, fibroblastic**; subtype does not change treatment.
- Grows through the cortex and lifts periosteum; spreads within the medulla (**skip metastases** in about 5-10% of patients, i.e. discontinuous foci in the same or transarticular bone) and **haematogenously** (lymph node spread rare).
- **Lungs are the commonest site of metastasis** (about 80-90% of metastatic cases), then bone. About 15-20% have detectable metastases at presentation, but about 80% have micrometastases, which is why surgery alone gave only 10-20% survival before chemotherapy.

### Clinical features
- **Pain** (initially activity-related, then constant and at night), swelling, warmth, restricted joint movement; pathological fracture in about 5-10%.
- Often attributed to sports injury, causing diagnostic delay.
- **Serum alkaline phosphatase and LDH:** raised in about half; **high LDH or ALP indicates worse prognosis**, and ALP is used to monitor relapse.

### Radiology
- **Metaphyseal, poorly defined, permeative, mixed lytic-sclerotic** lesion with a wide zone of transition.
- **Cloud-like osteoid matrix** in the soft tissue mass.
- **Periosteal reactions:** **Codman triangle** (elevated periosteum at the edge; seen in any aggressive lesion, not specific), **sunburst** (spiculated radiating) pattern, interrupted lamellar reaction.
- **MRI:** extent of marrow involvement and **skip lesions** (image the **whole bone and adjacent joint**), physeal and epiphyseal involvement, joint invasion, neurovascular encasement - all decide whether limb salvage is possible.
- **CT chest** for lung nodules; bone scintigraphy or **PET-CT** for skeletal metastases.

### Prognostic factors
| Factor | Unfavourable |
|---|---|
| **Metastases at diagnosis** | **Most important adverse factor** (5-year survival about 20-30%; better if lung only and resectable) |
| **Histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Huvos)** | **Less than 90% tumour necrosis = poor responder** |
| Site | Axial / pelvic tumours |
| Size | Large volume tumours (T2) |
| Surgical margin | Inadequate margin raises local recurrence |
| Laboratory | Raised LDH and ALP |
| Skip lesions | Behave like metastatic disease |

### Huvos (Rosen-Huvos) grading of chemotherapy response
| Grade | Necrosis | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Little or no effect (under 50%) | Poor responder |
| **II** | 50-89% | Poor responder |
| **III** | 90-99% | **Good responder** |
| **IV** | 100% (no viable tumour) | **Good responder** |

### Management
1. **Neoadjuvant (pre-operative) chemotherapy** for about 10 weeks: **MAP = high-dose Methotrexate (with leucovorin/folinic acid rescue), doxorubicin (Adriamycin) and cisPlatin**. This was developed from the **Rosen T-10 protocol** at Memorial Sloan Kettering.
2. **Restaging** with MRI and CT chest.
3. **Surgery with wide margins**: limb salvage in about 85-90% of patients today.
4. **Adjuvant (post-operative) chemotherapy** continuing MAP (total treatment about 29-30 weeks); the resected specimen gives the Huvos response grade.
5. **Pulmonary metastasectomy** for resectable lung metastases (at presentation or relapse) improves survival; it is a standard part of treatment.

- **Chemotherapy toxicities:** methotrexate (renal failure, mucositis; monitor levels, glucarpidase if delayed clearance), doxorubicin (**cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy**; dexrazoxane is cardioprotective), cisplatin (**ototoxicity**, nephrotoxicity, neuropathy), ifosfamide (haemorrhagic cystitis, prevented by **mesna**; Fanconi-type nephrotoxicity).
- **Radiotherapy:** osteosarcoma is **relatively radioresistant**; used only for unresectable tumours (spine, pelvis, skull) or palliation, often as proton or carbon-ion therapy.
- **Survival:** localised extremity disease with modern treatment about **65-70% at 5 years**; metastatic about 20-30%. Survival has not improved substantially since the 1980s.

### Landmark trials and evidence
- **MIOS (Multi-Institutional Osteosarcoma Study, Link et al., NEJM 1986)**: randomised trial showing that **adjuvant chemotherapy dramatically improves relapse-free survival** (about 66% versus 17% at 2 years) compared with surgery alone. Established chemotherapy as standard.
- **Simon et al. (MSTS, JBJS 1986)**: **limb salvage for distal femoral osteosarcoma gave survival equal to amputation** when wide margins were obtained.
- **EURAMOS-1 (published 2015-2016)**: largest osteosarcoma trial. In **poor responders**, adding **ifosfamide and etoposide (MAPIE)** to MAP **did not improve event-free survival** and increased toxicity. In **good responders**, adding **pegylated interferon alfa-2b** to MAP gave no significant benefit. Conclusion: **MAP remains the standard for all**, and post-operative chemotherapy should not be changed on the basis of poor response.
- **INT-0133 (Children's Oncology Group)**: **mifamurtide (MTP-PE, liposomal muramyl tripeptide)**, an immune macrophage activator, improved overall survival when added to chemotherapy (results debated); **approved in Europe, not by the US FDA**.
- Targeted therapy: multi-kinase inhibitors (regorafenib, cabozantinib) show modest activity in relapsed disease only.

### Surgical options
- **Limb salvage (contraindications are relative):** major neurovascular encasement that cannot be reconstructed, extensive soft tissue contamination (e.g. poorly placed biopsy, displaced pathological fracture through tumour), infection, very young child with large predicted leg-length discrepancy (now often managed with growing prostheses).
- **Reconstruction after resection:**
  - **Modular endoprosthesis (megaprosthesis)**: commonest; rotating-hinge knee for distal femur or proximal tibia.
  - **Expandable (growing) prosthesis** in skeletally immature children: non-invasive magnetic lengthening types avoid repeated surgery.
  - **Allograft** (osteoarticular or intercalary), **allograft-prosthesis composite**, vascularised fibula, recycled autograft (irradiated, frozen in liquid nitrogen or pasteurised).
  - **Rotationplasty (Van Nes)**: for distal femoral tumours in young children; the distal leg is rotated **180 degrees** and attached to the femur so that the **ankle functions as a knee** (plantarflexion = knee extension) and the foot fits a below-knee type prosthesis. Durable, active, no prosthetic loosening; cosmetic appearance is the main drawback.
  - **Amputation:** above-knee or hip disarticulation when limb salvage cannot achieve wide margins; same survival as limb salvage.
- **Proximal tibial resection:** the **extensor mechanism must be reconstructed** (medial gastrocnemius rotational flap with patellar tendon reattachment), and the gastrocnemius flap also covers the implant, reducing infection.
- **Endoprosthetic failure (Henderson classification):** type 1 **soft tissue failure** (instability, tendon failure), type 2 **aseptic loosening**, type 3 **structural failure** (implant or periprosthetic fracture), type 4 **infection**, type 5 **tumour progression**. Infection is the most feared and is particularly common after proximal tibial and pelvic reconstruction.
- **Local recurrence** after limb salvage is about 5-10% and carries a poor prognosis.
- **Follow-up:** CT chest and limb imaging every 3 months in years 1-2, then less frequently to 10 years; monitor late effects (cardiac, renal, hearing, fertility, second malignancy).

> Exam pearl: Conventional osteosarcoma: adolescent distal femoral metaphysis, mixed lytic-sclerotic with Codman triangle and sunburst. MAP neoadjuvant chemotherapy, wide resection, adjuvant MAP. Most important prognostic factor = metastases at diagnosis; next = Huvos necrosis (90% or more = good responder). EURAMOS-1: intensifying chemotherapy for poor responders does not help.

## 6. Subtypes of osteosarcoma
| Subtype | Key features | Treatment and prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| **Telangiectatic** | Purely lytic, expansile, haemorrhagic; **fluid-fluid levels on MRI mimic ABC**; malignant cells in the septa (thick, nodular, enhancing septa on MRI) | As conventional (chemotherapy + wide resection); prognosis similar to conventional; pathological fracture common |
| **Small cell** | Small round cells producing lace-like osteoid; may be CD99 positive | **Main differential is Ewing sarcoma** (no EWSR1 translocation); treated as conventional; slightly worse prognosis |
| **Low-grade central** | Metaphysis of femur or tibia, adults 20-40; slowly growing; **mimics fibrous dysplasia**; **MDM2 and CDK4 amplification** | **Wide excision alone**; no chemotherapy; excellent prognosis unless it dedifferentiates |
| **Parosteal** | Commonest surface OS (about 5% of all OS); **posterior distal femoral metaphysis** (popliteal surface); women 20-40 years; dense, lobulated mass **"wrapped around" the bone**; **radiolucent cleavage line (string sign)** between tumour and cortex; **MDM2/CDK4 amplification**; low grade | **Wide excision alone**; 5-year survival about 90%; marginal excision recurs; **dedifferentiated parosteal OS** (about 15-25%) is high-grade and treated as conventional |
| **Periosteal** | Surface of the **diaphysis of tibia or femur**, adolescents; **predominantly chondroblastic**, intermediate grade; saucerised cortex with **perpendicular "hair-on-end" spicules** and Codman triangle; medulla spared | Wide excision; **role of chemotherapy debated** (often given); prognosis better than conventional, worse than parosteal |
| **High-grade surface** | Rare, surface lesion but histologically like conventional | As conventional (chemotherapy + surgery) |
| **Secondary** (Paget, irradiation, infarct) | Older patients | Chemotherapy often poorly tolerated; poor prognosis |
| **Extraskeletal osteosarcoma** | Soft tissue of thigh in adults over 50 | Treated like soft tissue sarcoma; poor prognosis |

- **Parosteal versus myositis ossificans (most important differential):**
  - **Myositis ossificans:** **zonal pattern** with **mature bone at the periphery and immature centre**; history of trauma; matures over 6-8 weeks; separated from cortex.
  - **Parosteal osteosarcoma:** **densest centrally at the base**, less mature at the periphery (reverse zonal pattern); attached to cortex by a broad base.
  - Also differentiate from osteochondroma (corticomedullary continuity, cartilage cap) and **BPOP** (bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation, hands and feet).

> Exam pearl: Parosteal OS = posterior distal femur, woman 20-40, "string sign", MDM2 amplification, low grade, wide excision only, about 90% survival. Periosteal OS = tibial diaphysis, chondroblastic, hair-on-end. Telangiectatic OS = fluid-fluid levels like ABC but with thick nodular septa - never curette an "ABC" without histology.

## 7. Summary of radiological differentials for a bone-forming lesion
| Lesion | Discriminating feature |
|---|---|
| **Stress fracture** | Linear periosteal/endosteal reaction, no soft tissue mass, history of activity |
| **Exuberant callus** | History of fracture, matures over weeks |
| **Osteomyelitis** | Sequestrum, cloaca, systemic features; can mimic Ewing or OS |
| **Ewing sarcoma** | Diaphyseal, onion-skin periosteal reaction, large soft tissue mass, no osteoid matrix |
| **Osteoblastic metastasis** | Older patient, multiple lesions (prostate, breast) |
| **Paget disease** | Coarsened trabeculae, cortical thickening, bone enlargement, starts at an end of the bone and advances (blade of grass / flame-shaped front in long bones) |

cartilage tumours.md:
## 1. Overview
- **Chondrogenic tumours** form hyaline cartilage matrix. Radiographic hallmark of cartilage matrix: **"rings and arcs" / "popcorn" / punctate (stippled) calcification**.
- **WHO 2020 classification (bone):**
  - **Benign:** osteochondroma, enchondroma, periosteal chondroma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, subungual exostosis, bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (BPOP), synovial chondromatosis, osteochondromyxoma.
  - **Intermediate (locally aggressive):** **atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT)** of the appendicular skeleton (formerly grade 1 chondrosarcoma).
  - **Malignant:** chondrosarcoma grades 1-3 (grade 1 term kept for **axial skeleton**: pelvis, scapula, skull base), periosteal chondrosarcoma, **clear cell**, **mesenchymal** and **dedifferentiated** chondrosarcoma.
- **Location in bone (classic exam table):**

| Location | Cartilage lesion |
|---|---|
| **Epiphysis, skeletally immature** | **Chondroblastoma** |
| **Epiphysis, adult** | **Clear cell chondrosarcoma** (and GCT, which is not cartilaginous) |
| **Metaphysis, eccentric** | **Chondromyxoid fibroma**, osteochondroma |
| **Medullary metaphysis/diaphysis** | Enchondroma, central chondrosarcoma |
| **Surface** | Osteochondroma, periosteal chondroma, periosteal chondrosarcoma |
| **Short tubular bones of the hand** | Enchondroma (commonest primary bone tumour of the hand) |

- **Molecular high-yield:** **IDH1/IDH2 mutations** in enchondroma, Ollier, Maffucci and about 50% of central (conventional and dedifferentiated) chondrosarcomas; **EXT1/EXT2** in osteochondroma and HME; **H3F3B K36M (H3.3)** in chondroblastoma; **GRM1** rearrangement in chondromyxoid fibroma; **HEY1-NCOA2** fusion in mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.

## 2. Osteochondroma (osteocartilaginous exostosis)
### Pathology and epidemiology
- **Commonest benign bone tumour** (about one third of benign bone tumours; many unrecognised). Age 10-30, slight male predominance.
- A **developmental lesion**: physeal cartilage herniates through the periosteal bone collar (perichondral ring of LaCroix) and grows at right angles to the bone.
- **Defining feature: cortical and medullary continuity with the host bone**, capped by hyaline cartilage. It grows by enchondral ossification under the cap and **stops growing at skeletal maturity**.
- **Sites:** metaphysis of long bones, especially **distal femur, proximal tibia (around the knee) and proximal humerus**; points **away from the adjacent joint** (grows along tendon pull). Sessile or pedunculated.
- Radiation can induce osteochondromas (e.g. after childhood irradiation).

### Clinical features and complications
- Painless hard mass; pain from **overlying bursa (bursitis)**, tendon snapping, **fracture of the stalk**.
- **Neurovascular compression:** **common peroneal nerve** at the proximal fibula; **popliteal artery pseudoaneurysm** or thrombosis from distal femoral or proximal tibial lesions.
- Growth disturbance and deformity (especially in multiple exostoses), spinal cord compression (rare spinal lesions).
- **Malignant transformation to secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma:** **about 1% for solitary lesions**; **about 1-5% (lifetime) in HME** (older figures up to 10-20% are overestimates; debated). Pelvis, scapula and proximal femur lesions are the highest risk.
- **Warning signs of malignancy:** **growth or new pain after skeletal maturity**, **cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm in an adult** (some use 1.5 cm) on MRI, irregular cap with lucent areas or soft tissue mass with scattered calcification, cortical destruction of the stalk.
  - In growing children, caps up to 3 cm can be normal.

### Treatment
- **Observation** for asymptomatic lesions.
- **Excision** for pain, neurovascular compression, cosmesis, deformity or suspicion of malignancy: **remove the whole cartilage cap with its perichondrium** (and stalk base) to prevent recurrence. Ideally after skeletal maturity to reduce recurrence and avoid physeal damage.
- **Peroneal nerve** must be identified and protected when excising proximal fibular lesions.
- Suspected malignant change: biopsy-guided **wide en bloc resection** (do not shell out).

### Hereditary multiple exostoses (HME, multiple osteochondromas)
- **Autosomal dominant**, high penetrance (about 96%); **EXT1 (chromosome 8q24)** gives a more severe phenotype than **EXT2 (11p)**. EXT genes encode glycosyltransferases for **heparan sulphate** synthesis.
- **Short stature**, limb length discrepancy, **genu valgum** (proximal tibia), **ankle valgus** (distal tibia and fibular shortening), **coxa valga** and hip subluxation.
- **Forearm deformity (in 40-60%)**: the **ulna is short** (lesions at the distal ulna), radius bowed with ulnar inclination of the distal radius, ulnar translation of the carpus, and **radial head dislocation**.
- **Masada classification of the forearm:**

| Type | Description | Management idea |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Osteochondroma of distal ulna; ulna short; radius bowed; radial head **not** dislocated | Excision + ulnar lengthening (gradual distraction) ± radial corrective osteotomy |
| **IIa** | Radial head dislocated, with an osteochondroma of the proximal radius | Excision; radial head excision at maturity if painful |
| **IIb** | Radial head dislocated secondary to a short ulna (distal ulnar lesion), no proximal radial lesion | Ulnar lengthening ± open reduction of radial head (difficult) |
| **III** | Osteochondroma of distal radius with relative shortening of the radius | Excision |

- **Treatment principles in HME:** excise symptomatic lesions, **guided growth (hemiepiphysiodesis)** for genu valgum and ankle valgus, lengthening for forearm and limb discrepancy, lifelong awareness of malignant change (new pain or growth in adulthood).
- **Related conditions:**
  - **Trevor disease (dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica):** intra-articular **epiphyseal osteochondroma**, usually on the **medial side** of one lower limb (talus, distal tibia, distal femur); boys about 3:1. Excise symptomatic lesions; preserve articular surface.
  - **Metachondromatosis:** AD, **PTPN11**; both exostoses (which **point towards the joint**, mainly hands and feet) and enchondromas; lesions may regress.
  - **Subungual exostosis (Dupuytren):** distal phalanx of the great toe, trauma-related, **no medullary continuity**; excise with cap.
  - **BPOP (Nora lesion):** surface lesion of hands and feet, no corticomedullary continuity, high recurrence.

> Exam pearl: Osteochondroma = corticomedullary continuity + cartilage cap, points away from the joint, stops growing at maturity. Cap over 2 cm in an adult or growth/pain after maturity = suspect chondrosarcoma. HME = AD, EXT1 (8q24, worse) / EXT2 (11p), heparan sulphate, short ulna with radial head dislocation (Masada).

## 3. Enchondroma and enchondromatoses
### Solitary enchondroma
- Benign intramedullary hyaline cartilage, probably from physeal rests. Age 20-50. Often an incidental finding.
- **Commonest primary bone tumour of the hand** (about half occur in the hand): **proximal phalanx** most common, then metacarpals and middle phalanges. Also proximal humerus, distal femur and proximal tibia (metaphysis to diaphysis).
- **Hand:** presents with **pathological fracture** after minor trauma; expansile lytic lesion with thinned cortex and stippled calcification.
  - **Management:** allow the fracture to heal (about 4-6 weeks), then **curettage ± bone graft** or bone substitute (some treat in one stage). Recurrence is uncommon. Malignant change in the hand is very rare.
- **Long bones:** central lesion with **rings-and-arcs calcification**, little or no endosteal scalloping, no cortical breach, no soft tissue mass, usually painless.
  - Painless lesions without aggressive features: **observation with serial imaging** (radiographs or MRI).

### Enchondroma versus atypical cartilaginous tumour / low-grade chondrosarcoma in long bones
| Feature | Favours enchondroma | Favours ACT / chondrosarcoma |
|---|---|---|
| **Pain** | Absent (pain usually from another cause, e.g. knee OA) | **Pain attributable to the lesion**, especially at night |
| **Endosteal scalloping** | Absent or shallow | **Deep (more than two thirds of cortical thickness)** and long (over two thirds of lesion length) |
| **Cortex** | Normal | **Cortical thickening, expansion, breach** |
| **Periosteal reaction / soft tissue mass** | Absent | Present |
| **Size** | Usually under 5 cm | Larger (often over 5 cm) |
| **Bone scan uptake** | Mild | Greater than the anterior iliac crest |
| **Site** | Hand, long bones | **Axial skeleton (pelvis) almost always malignant** |
| **Histology** | Hypocellular lobules **encasing** host trabeculae | **Permeation and entrapment of host trabeculae**, myxoid change, increased cellularity |

- Histology alone is unreliable for distinguishing enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma (high interobserver variability); **clinical, radiological and pathological correlation** is required.
- **Bone infarct** (differential): **serpiginous peripheral sclerotic rim** ("smoke rising up a chimney"), no scalloping, no central rings and arcs.

### Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome
| Condition | Features | Malignancy risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Ollier disease (enchondromatosis)** | **Multiple enchondromas**, often **unilateral predominance**, sporadic (not inherited), **somatic mosaic IDH1/IDH2** mutations; limb shortening, angular deformity, short ulna with forearm bowing, hand deformity | **Secondary central chondrosarcoma in about 25-40%** (figures vary; debated) |
| **Maffucci syndrome** | Multiple enchondromas + **soft tissue (spindle cell) haemangiomas** (blue nodules with **phleboliths** on radiographs); IDH1/IDH2 | **Higher (up to about 50%)**, plus **non-skeletal malignancies** (gliomas, ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumour, pancreatic and hepatic tumours) |

- Lifelong surveillance; any new pain or growth needs MRI and evaluation.
- Limb deformity: corrective osteotomies, gradual lengthening (Ilizarov / hexapod); lesions within distraction regenerate ossify.

### Periosteal (juxtacortical) chondroma
- Surface cartilage lesion under the periosteum, young adults, **proximal humerus** commonest, hand.
- **Saucerisation of the cortex with a sclerotic buttress**, no medullary involvement; usually **under 3 cm**.
- Differential: **periosteal chondrosarcoma** (larger, usually over 3-5 cm, older patients, invasion of cortex/medulla).
- Treatment: **marginal en bloc excision** with the underlying cortex; low recurrence.

## 4. Chondroblastoma
- About 1% of bone tumours. **Age 10-25 (skeletally immature)**; male predominance about 2:1.
- **Epiphysis or apophysis** (equivalent): **proximal humerus (Codman tumour)**, **distal femur**, **proximal tibia**, **greater trochanter**; also **talus and calcaneus** in older patients.
- **Symptoms:** joint pain, effusion, stiffness (mimics intra-articular pathology).
- **Radiograph:** small, round, well-defined **lytic epiphyseal lesion with a thin sclerotic rim**, central calcification in about a third to half; may cross the physis into the metaphysis.
- **MRI:** **extensive surrounding marrow and soft tissue oedema** and periosteal reaction (out of proportion to the lesion); **secondary ABC** change in about 15-30% (fluid-fluid levels).
- **Histology:** polygonal **chondroblasts with grooved "coffee-bean" nuclei**, scattered osteoclast-like giant cells, pink chondroid matrix, **"chicken-wire" pericellular calcification**. Immunohistochemistry: S100, SOX9, DOG1 and **H3 K36M mutant-specific antibody** (H3F3B).
- **Treatment:** **extended curettage** (high-speed burr ± phenol, cryotherapy or argon adjuvant) and grafting or cementing, approached to protect the **physis and articular cartilage** (e.g. through the metaphysis or via a cortical window). **Local recurrence about 10-20%** (higher in pelvis, hip, talus, and with secondary ABC). RFA for small lesions in difficult sites.
- **Benign lung metastases** in about 1-2% (usually after local recurrence); treated by excision, good prognosis.
- **Differentials (epiphyseal lucent lesions):** GCT (skeletally mature, no sclerotic rim, extends to subchondral bone), clear cell chondrosarcoma (adult), infection (Brodie abscess can be epiphyseal in children), LCH, intraosseous ganglion, subchondral cyst/geode.

## 5. Chondromyxoid fibroma (CMF)
- **Rarest benign cartilage tumour** (under 1% of bone tumours). Age 10-30.
- **Metaphysis of the proximal tibia** is the classic site (about one third around the knee), also distal femur, pelvis, feet.
- **Radiograph:** **eccentric, elongated, lobulated lytic metaphyseal lesion** with a **sclerotic scalloped ("bite-like") margin**, cortical expansion, **calcification uncommon** (unlike other cartilage lesions).
- **Histology:** lobules of **stellate and spindle cells in myxoid and chondroid stroma**, hypocellular centres with hypercellular periphery; **GRM1** rearrangement.
- **Differentials:** NOF (also eccentric metaphyseal, but cortical, multiloculated, children), ABC, fibrous dysplasia, chondrosarcoma (histological mimic).
- **Treatment:** **extended curettage with adjuvant and bone grafting**; recurrence about 15-25%; en bloc resection for expendable bones.

## 6. Chondrosarcoma
### Epidemiology and classification
- **Second commonest primary malignant bone tumour** (about 20-30%). **Adults 40-70 years**, slight male predominance. Rare in children (consider mesenchymal subtype).
- **Sites:** **pelvis (ilium) commonest**, then **proximal femur**, **proximal humerus**, ribs and scapula. Flat bones and proximal limb bones (unlike enchondroma, which favours the hand).
- **Classification by origin:**
  - **Primary central (conventional)**: about 85-90%; arises de novo in the medulla.
  - **Secondary central**: from enchondroma (Ollier, Maffucci).
  - **Secondary peripheral**: from the cap of an osteochondroma (solitary or HME); usually low grade; treated by wide excision.
  - **Periosteal chondrosarcoma**: surface.
- **Subtypes:** dedifferentiated (about 10%), clear cell (about 2%), mesenchymal (about 2-3%).

### Clinical and radiology
- **Pain (often deep, dull, nocturnal) is the key symptom**; mass in pelvic lesions often large at presentation; pathological fracture in high grade.
- **Radiograph and CT:** lytic expansile lesion with **rings-and-arcs calcification**, **deep endosteal scalloping**, **cortical thickening**, cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, soft tissue mass. A **purely lytic area within a calcified cartilage lesion suggests dedifferentiation** (target the biopsy there).
- **MRI:** lobulated, **very high T2 signal** (hyaline cartilage), peripheral and septal ("ring and arc") enhancement; defines extent and soft tissue mass.
- **Staging:** CT chest, bone scan or PET-CT. Biopsy from the most aggressive area (CT/MRI guided), at the treating centre.

### Grading and prognosis
| Grade | Histology | Metastasis | Approximate 10-year survival |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACT / grade 1** | Low cellularity, mild atypia, abundant hyaline matrix | Rare | About 90% |
| **Grade 2** | More cellular, myxoid change, nuclear atypia, mitoses rare | About 10-30% | About 60-70% |
| **Grade 3** | Highly cellular, pleomorphic, mitoses, myxoid | Up to 70% | About 30-50% |
| **Dedifferentiated** | Low-grade cartilage **abruptly juxtaposed with high-grade non-cartilaginous sarcoma** (osteosarcoma, UPS, fibrosarcoma) | High | **5-year survival about 10-25%** |

- **Grade is the most important prognostic factor**; others: margin status (local recurrence), axial site, size.
- Lungs are the commonest metastatic site.

### Management
- **Conventional chondrosarcoma is resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy** (low mitotic rate, poor vascularity, abundant matrix), so **surgery is the mainstay**.
- **ACT of long bones (intracompartmental, no soft tissue extension):** **extended intralesional curettage with local adjuvant** (high-speed burr, phenol, liquid nitrogen cryotherapy, argon, or ethanol) and cement or graft; local recurrence low (about 5%), with better function than resection. Small asymptomatic lesions are increasingly managed by **active surveillance** (debated).
- **Grade 1 axial (pelvis, scapula, skull base), grade 2, grade 3, and secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma:** **wide en bloc resection**. Intralesional surgery leads to recurrence, and recurrent tumours can be of higher grade.
  - **Pelvic chondrosarcoma (Enneking-Dunham pelvic resection zones):** **I = ilium, II = periacetabular, III = pubis and ischium (obturator ring), IV = sacral extension**. Periacetabular (zone II) resections require reconstruction (custom or modular pelvic prosthesis, ice-cream-cone implants, allograft, hip transposition) or are left as a flail hip; **hindquarter amputation** if wide margins cannot otherwise be achieved.
- **Radiotherapy:** for incomplete resection, inoperable sites (skull base, spine) using high-dose **proton or carbon-ion therapy**; palliation.
- **Chemotherapy:** only for **mesenchymal** (Ewing-type regimens) and **dedifferentiated** chondrosarcoma (osteosarcoma-type regimens; benefit debated), and metastatic disease in trials. **IDH1 inhibitors (ivosidenib)** are under study for IDH-mutant tumours.
- **Follow-up:** long term (10 years or more) because of late local recurrence and lung metastases.

### Other subtypes
| Subtype | Key features | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Clear cell chondrosarcoma** | Low grade; **epiphysis of proximal femur (about two thirds) or proximal humerus**; adults 25-50, males; well-defined lytic epiphyseal lesion; **mimics chondroblastoma** but in a skeletally mature patient; clear cells with osteoclast-like giant cells | **Wide en bloc resection** (curettage leads to high recurrence); late metastases possible, long follow-up |
| **Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma** | Young (10-30); jaw, ribs, spine, pelvis, and **extraskeletal** (meninges); **biphasic: undifferentiated small round blue cells with islands of hyaline cartilage**, haemangiopericytoma-like vessels; **HEY1-NCOA2** fusion; CD99 positive (differential: Ewing) | Wide resection + **chemotherapy** (Ewing-type) ± radiotherapy; poor prognosis, late metastases |
| **Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma** | Older (50-70); pelvis, femur, humerus; **bimorphic** pattern; lytic aggressive component next to calcified cartilage; pathological fracture common | Wide resection or amputation ± chemotherapy; very poor prognosis |
| **Periosteal chondrosarcoma** | Surface of femur/humerus; usually **over 5 cm**; invades cortex | Wide excision; good prognosis (low grade) |

> Exam pearl: Chondrosarcoma: adult, pelvis commonest, painful lesion with rings-and-arcs calcification and deep endosteal scalloping. Chemo- and radio-resistant; grade is the key prognostic factor. Appendicular ACT = extended curettage + adjuvant; axial grade 1 and all grade 2/3 = wide resection. Clear cell CS = adult epiphysis of proximal femur (chondroblastoma look-alike). Mesenchymal CS = small round cells + cartilage, HEY1-NCOA2, chemotherapy-sensitive. Dedifferentiated = bimorphic, worst prognosis.

## 7. Synovial chondromatosis
- Classified with cartilage tumours (WHO 2020) as a benign, locally aggressive neoplasm of the synovium (**FN1-ACVR2A / FN1 rearrangements**).
- Monoarticular, adults 30-50, **knee commonest**, then hip, elbow, shoulder.
- Multiple cartilaginous nodules in the synovium that detach as loose bodies and may calcify (**multiple uniform-sized "rice-grain" ossified loose bodies**); erosion of bone on both sides of the joint.
- **Milgram stages:** **I** active intrasynovial disease, no loose bodies; **II** transitional, synovial nodules and loose bodies; **III** multiple loose bodies, quiescent synovium.
- **Treatment:** **loose body removal + synovectomy** (open or arthroscopic); recurrence about 10-20%. Malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is rare (under about 5%), suspected with rapid recurrence or marrow invasion.
- Differentials: PVNS (haemosiderin, blooming on gradient-echo MRI, no calcification), secondary osteochondromatosis (loose bodies of varying size from OA).

## 8. Quick comparison table of cartilage tumours
| Lesion | Age | Site | Discriminating clue |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Osteochondroma** | 10-30 | Metaphysis around knee | Corticomedullary continuity, points away from joint |
| **Enchondroma** | 20-50 | Hand phalanges, long bone medulla | Pathological fracture of proximal phalanx; rings-and-arcs |
| **Chondroblastoma** | 10-25 | **Epiphysis**, proximal humerus | Chicken-wire calcification, coffee-bean nuclei, oedema on MRI |
| **Chondromyxoid fibroma** | 10-30 | Proximal tibial metaphysis, eccentric | Scalloped sclerotic rim, little calcification |
| **Chondrosarcoma** | 40-70 | Pelvis, proximal femur/humerus | Pain, deep endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening |
| **Clear cell CS** | 25-50 | Epiphysis proximal femur | Adult "chondroblastoma" |
| **Mesenchymal CS** | 10-30 | Jaw, ribs, extraskeletal | Small round cells + cartilage |

giant cell and cystic lesions.md:
## 1. Approach to a lytic (lucent) bone lesion
- **Four questions:** age of patient, location in the bone (epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis; central, eccentric, cortical), margin (zone of transition), matrix and periosteal reaction. Number of lesions.
- **Lodwick classification of margins (rate of growth):**

| Grade | Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **IA** | Geographic, **sclerotic rim** | Slow growing, benign (NOF, UBC, fibrous dysplasia) |
| **IB** | Geographic, well-defined, **no sclerotic rim** | Faster (GCT, myeloma) |
| **IC** | Geographic, **ill-defined margin** | Aggressive |
| **II** | **Moth-eaten** | Aggressive (infection, lymphoma, metastasis) |
| **III** | **Permeative** (wide zone of transition) | Very aggressive: Ewing, lymphoma, osteomyelitis |

- **Epiphyseal lucent lesions:** chondroblastoma (immature), **GCT** (mature), clear cell chondrosarcoma, infection, LCH, intraosseous ganglion, subchondral cyst (geode).
- **Multiple lesions in an adult:** metastases, myeloma, brown tumours, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, enchondromatosis.
- **Fluid-fluid levels on MRI (not specific):** **ABC (primary or secondary), telangiectatic osteosarcoma**, GCT, chondroblastoma, UBC after fracture.
- **Giant-cell-rich lesions (histological differential):** GCT, **brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism**, ABC, chondroblastoma, NOF, giant cell reparative granuloma (jaw, hands and feet), giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma, pigmented villonodular synovitis extending into bone.
- **Rule:** a "benign-looking" cystic lesion with solid enhancing areas, thick nodular septa, cortical destruction or soft tissue mass needs a **biopsy before curettage** (telangiectatic OS can mimic ABC).

## 2. Giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB)
### Epidemiology and pathology
- About **5% of primary bone tumours** and about 20% of benign bone tumours; **more common in Asian (including Indian and Chinese) populations**.
- **Age 20-40, after physeal closure** (about 80%); rare under 15 (if so, may be metaphyseal). **Slight female predominance**.
- **Sites:** **distal femur > proximal tibia > distal radius** (third commonest, and most aggressive with highest recurrence) > **sacrum** (commonest axial site; the vertebral body above the sacrum is uncommon) > proximal humerus. About 50-60% around the knee. Multicentric GCT is rare (under 1%; consider hyperparathyroidism and hand involvement).
- **Pathology:**
  - **Neoplastic cells = mononuclear stromal cells** (osteoblast-lineage), which express **RANKL**; they carry the **H3F3A (H3.3) G34W mutation in over 90%** (immunostain H3.3 G34W is diagnostic).
  - **Osteoclast-like giant cells** (expressing **RANK**) are reactive; they are recruited by RANKL and resorb bone. Their nuclei resemble the stromal cell nuclei.
  - **This RANKL-RANK pathway is the basis of denosumab therapy.**
- Classified by WHO as **intermediate, locally aggressive, rarely metastasising**.

### Clinical
- Pain, swelling near a joint, effusion, reduced movement; **pathological fracture in about 10-30%**.

### Imaging
- **Eccentric, lytic, epiphyseo-metaphyseal lesion extending up to the subchondral bone** (within about 1 cm of the articular surface).
- **Geographic, non-sclerotic margin (Lodwick IB)**, no matrix mineralisation, cortical expansion and thinning, "soap-bubble" appearance from ridges, cortical breach and soft tissue mass in aggressive cases. Periosteal reaction unusual.
- **MRI:** low-to-intermediate T2 signal in solid areas (haemosiderin and collagen), fluid-fluid levels from secondary ABC change (about 15%); defines soft tissue extension and joint involvement.
- **CT chest at diagnosis** (lung metastases).
- **Bloods:** **serum calcium, phosphate and PTH** to exclude **brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism**, especially with multiple lesions, unusual sites or giant cells in the jaw/hands.

### Campanacci radiographic grading (corresponds to Enneking benign stages 1-3)
| Grade | Radiographic features | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **I (latent)** | Well-marginated, **thin sclerotic rim**, cortex intact | Rare; extended curettage |
| **II (active)** | Well-defined margin **without sclerotic rim**, cortex thinned and expanded but intact | Commonest (about 70-80%); **extended curettage + adjuvant + cement** |
| **III (aggressive)** | **Indistinct margins, cortical breach, soft tissue mass** | Higher recurrence; curettage still possible if joint salvageable, otherwise **en bloc resection** and reconstruction |

### Management
#### Extended (intralesional) curettage: treatment of choice for most
1. **Large cortical window** (as big as the lesion) so every recess can be seen directly.
2. Thorough **curettage**, then **high-speed burr** of all walls.
3. **Local adjuvant** to extend the margin: **phenol**, **liquid nitrogen cryotherapy**, **argon beam coagulation**, hydrogen peroxide or absolute alcohol; pulsed lavage.
4. **Filling the cavity with PMMA bone cement**: exothermic polymerisation kills residual cells (about 2-3 mm), gives immediate structural support and allows early weight bearing, and makes **recurrence easy to detect** (expanding lucency at the cement-bone interface). Subchondral bone graft beneath the cement to protect articular cartilage is optional (debated). Internal fixation (plate) if the defect weakens the bone.
- **Recurrence rates:** curettage alone historically **about 40-60%**; extended curettage with burr and adjuvant **about 10-20%**. Most recurrences appear **within 2-3 years**; distal radius, Campanacci III and soft tissue extension recur more often.
- **Pathological fracture** is not an automatic indication for resection; if the fracture is not grossly displaced into the joint, curettage can be done (after or with fixation).

#### En bloc (wide) resection
- **Indications:** extensive destruction with an unsalvageable joint, large soft tissue component (Campanacci III), grossly displaced intra-articular pathological fracture, multiply recurrent tumour, and **expendable bones** (proximal fibula, distal ulna, rib, iliac wing, coccyx).
- Lower recurrence (about 0-10%) but worse function.
- **Distal radius Campanacci III:** en bloc resection + reconstruction with **non-vascularised or vascularised proximal fibula autograft (osteoarticular, fibula head to the carpus)**, osteoarticular allograft, or **ulnar translocation with wrist arthrodesis** (radiocarpal fusion).
- Around the knee: megaprosthesis or osteoarticular allograft.

#### Spine and sacrum
- Sacral and spinal GCT are difficult: en bloc resection risks bowel, bladder and sexual dysfunction (sacral nerve roots).
- Options: **intralesional curettage + adjuvant with pre-operative embolisation**, **serial arterial embolisation**, **denosumab**, and **radiotherapy** (now reserved for unresectable disease because of the risk of **radiation-induced malignant transformation**, historically up to about 10%, lower with modern megavoltage techniques).

#### Medical therapy
- **Denosumab** (fully human monoclonal antibody against **RANKL**):
  - Dose: **120 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, with loading doses on days 8 and 15 of the first month**, with calcium and vitamin D supplements.
  - **FDA approved (2013)** for adults and skeletally mature adolescents with **unresectable GCT or where surgery would cause severe morbidity**, based on open-label phase 2 trials (Thomas et al., Lancet Oncology 2010; Chawla et al., 2013 and 2019) showing tumour response in most patients (loss of giant cells, new bone formation).
  - **Uses:** unresectable or sacral/spinal tumours, metastatic disease, and **neoadjuvant downstaging** to allow joint-preserving surgery (debated).
  - **Problems:**
    - **Higher local recurrence after curettage when used pre-operatively** (thick new bone and sclerotic rim hide residual tumour; stromal cells are not killed) - so for lesions already suitable for curettage, **go straight to surgery**.
    - **Recurrence or regrowth after stopping**, so long-term treatment may be needed (optimal duration unknown; dosing intervals are often extended).
    - **Osteonecrosis of the jaw** (about 1-5%, increasing with duration), **hypocalcaemia**, **atypical femoral fractures**, rebound hypercalcaemia in young patients after stopping, and **reports of malignant transformation** (sarcoma) during treatment.
- **Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid)** also inhibit osteoclast giant cells; used as a cheaper adjuvant to reduce recurrence and for unresectable disease (evidence weaker).
- **Interferon alfa** and radiotherapy for refractory cases.

### Metastases and malignancy
- **Lung metastases ("benign pulmonary implants") in about 2-5%**, usually 2-4 years after diagnosis and often after local recurrence (especially distal radius). Histologically identical to the primary; usually indolent. Treat by **metastasectomy**, observation or denosumab; good prognosis.
- **Malignancy in GCT (about 1-4%):**
  - **Primary malignant GCT:** high-grade sarcoma juxtaposed with conventional GCT at presentation.
  - **Secondary malignant GCT:** sarcoma at the site of previous GCT, usually **after radiotherapy** (or rarely after surgery or denosumab). Poor prognosis; treated like osteosarcoma.
- **Follow-up:** radiographs of the site and **chest imaging every 3-6 months for 2-3 years**, then annually to about 5-10 years.

> Exam pearl: GCT = skeletally mature, eccentric epiphyseo-metaphyseal lytic lesion reaching subchondral bone, non-sclerotic margin. Neoplastic cell = RANKL-expressing stromal cell (H3F3A G34W); giant cells are reactive. Distal femur > proximal tibia > distal radius (most aggressive); sacrum commonest axial site. Extended curettage + burr + adjuvant + PMMA (recurrence about 10-20%). Denosumab for unresectable disease - not routinely before curettage (more recurrence). Lung implants 2-5%. Always check calcium/PTH to exclude brown tumour.

## 3. Unicameral (simple) bone cyst (UBC)
### Features
- Fluid-filled cavity lined by a thin fibrous membrane; **not a true neoplasm** (although **NFATC2 fusions** have recently been described). Cause thought to be **venous obstruction** with fluid rich in prostaglandins, interleukin-1 and enzymes that resorb bone.
- **Age 5-15 years, male to female about 2:1**.
- **Sites:** **proximal humerus (about 50-60%)**, **proximal femur (about 25-30%)**; in adults, **calcaneus** (neutral triangle under the angle of Gissane) and ilium.
- **Pathological fracture is the commonest presentation (about two thirds to three quarters)**; otherwise incidental.

### Radiology
- **Central (not eccentric) metaphyseal lytic lesion**, **symmetrically expanded but not wider than the physis**, thin sclerotic margin, thinned cortex, no periosteal reaction without fracture, no matrix.
- **"Fallen fragment" sign** (a cortical fragment sinks to the dependent part of the fluid-filled cyst) is **pathognomonic** of UBC (versus solid lesions). The "rising bubble" sign is the gas equivalent.
- **Active vs latent:**

| Phase | Features | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| **Active** | **Within about 1 cm of (abutting) the physis**, usually **under 10-12 years** | High recurrence after treatment; risk of physeal growth arrest |
| **Latent (inactive)** | **Migrated away from the physis** into the diaphysis by normal growth (over 1 cm), older child | Lower recurrence; tends to heal |

- **Risk of fracture:** cyst index (cyst area / diaphyseal diameter squared) and thin cortex; fracture is likely when the cyst occupies most of the bone width.
- **Calcaneal UBC versus intraosseous lipoma:** lipoma has fat density and often a **central calcification ("cockade" / target)**; UBC has fluid content.
- **Differentials:** ABC (eccentric, expands wider than the physis, fluid-fluid levels, multiple septa), fibrous dysplasia (ground glass), LCH, enchondroma, NOF.

### Management
- **Fracture through a proximal humeral cyst:** treat the fracture non-operatively (sling); the fracture heals in about 6 weeks, but **the cyst heals after fracture in only about 10-15%**. Then decide on treatment of the cyst.
- **Observation** in older children with latent lesions and low fracture risk.
- **Minimally invasive options:**
  - **Aspiration + intralesional methylprednisolone acetate injection** (Scaglietti 1979); often **multiple injections** needed. Confirm with straw-coloured fluid and contrast cystogram (contrast stays in a single cavity).
  - Injection of **autologous bone marrow** or **demineralised bone matrix**, or calcium sulphate pellets.
  - **Decompression** (trephination / curettage with disruption of the cyst wall and canal communication) and **flexible intramedullary nails** (elastic stable intramedullary nails act as a continuous drain and give stability; allow early return to activity), or cannulated screws.
- **Evidence:** **Wright et al. (JBJS Am 2008), multicentre RCT: methylprednisolone injection gave a higher healing rate (about 42%) than bone marrow injection (about 23%)** at 2 years. Overall, no technique gives complete healing in every case; recurrence after any method is common (about 20-40%).
- **Open curettage and bone grafting** with or without adjuvant: for failed injections or large lesions; risk of **physeal injury** in active cysts.
- **Proximal femoral UBC:** high risk of fracture with **varus malunion, AVN and growth arrest** - so treat **surgically**: curettage + graft and **internal fixation** (flexible nails, pediatric hip screw or plate, avoiding the physis), especially for large cysts or after fracture.
- **Assessment of healing** (Neer/Cole type classifications): healed, healed with residual radiolucency, persistent, recurrent.

> Exam pearl: UBC = 5-15 years, proximal humerus, central metaphyseal, not wider than the physis, fallen fragment sign pathognomonic. Active = abutting the physis (under 1 cm), recurs more. Fracture heals but the cyst rarely heals. Steroid injection beat bone marrow injection in the Wright 2008 RCT. Proximal femur cysts need surgical fixation.

## 4. Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)
### Features
- **Blood-filled, multiloculated expansile lesion**; WHO intermediate, locally aggressive.
- **Age under 20 in about 80%** (peak 10-20), roughly equal sex distribution.
- **Sites:** metaphysis of long bones (**femur, tibia, humerus**), **spine (posterior elements, can extend into the body; about 15-20%)**, pelvis, sacrum.
- **Primary ABC (about 70%)**: true neoplasm with **USP6 gene rearrangement** (17p13; commonest partner **CDH11**). Also seen in **nodular fasciitis and myositis ossificans** (USP6 family).
- **Secondary ABC (about 30%)**: ABC-like change within another lesion, without USP6 rearrangement - **GCT** (commonest), **chondroblastoma**, **osteoblastoma**, fibrous dysplasia, NOF, UBC, and **telangiectatic osteosarcoma**. Treatment is that of the underlying lesion.
- **Solid variant (giant cell reparative granuloma-like)** is part of the same spectrum.

### Clinical and imaging
- Pain and swelling of short duration, pathological fracture; spine: back pain, scoliosis, **radiculopathy or cord compression**.
- **Radiograph:** **eccentric, expansile, "blow-out" lytic lesion** with a thin **eggshell** cortical rim, internal trabeculation ("soap bubble"), may expand **wider than the physis**; Codman triangle may be seen at the margins.
- **MRI: multiple fluid-fluid levels** (blood products of differing ages), **thin, smooth enhancing septa**.
- **Telangiectatic osteosarcoma must be excluded:** thick nodular enhancing septa, solid component, cortical destruction, soft tissue mass and aggressive margins favour TOS. **Biopsy of the septa and solid areas** before definitive treatment.
- **Histology:** blood-filled cavernous spaces separated by **fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclast-like giant cells and "blue bone"** (reactive woven bone); no endothelial lining.

### Management
| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Extended curettage + adjuvant (burr, phenol, cryotherapy, argon) + bone graft or cement** | Standard; **recurrence about 10-20%**, higher in young children and lesions near the physis; most recurrences within 2 years |
| **Percutaneous sclerotherapy** (**polidocanol**, doxycycline, alcohol) | Minimally invasive; multiple injections; an RCT (**Varshney et al. 2010**) found polidocanol gave healing comparable to curettage with fewer complications; increasingly used first line, especially in difficult sites |
| **Selective arterial embolisation** | Pelvis, sacrum and spine; as primary treatment or to reduce intra-operative bleeding before surgery |
| **Denosumab** | Unresectable spinal or sacral lesions; regrowth after stopping and **rebound hypercalcaemia in children** are concerns |
| **En bloc resection** | Expendable bones (fibula, rib) or recurrent aggressive lesions |
| **Spine** | Pre-operative embolisation, curettage or excision, decompression and **instrumented stabilisation** for instability or deficit |
| **Radiotherapy** | **Avoided** (risk of radiation-induced sarcoma, growth disturbance); last resort |

> Exam pearl: Primary ABC = USP6 (CDH11-USP6) rearrangement; secondary ABC commonest with GCT. Eccentric, expansile, eggshell rim, fluid-fluid levels. Must exclude telangiectatic osteosarcoma (thick nodular septa) by biopsy. Curettage + adjuvant recurs 10-20%; polidocanol sclerotherapy is an accepted alternative.

## 5. UBC versus ABC versus GCT
| Feature | UBC | ABC | GCT |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Age** | 5-15 | 10-20 | 20-40 (mature) |
| **Position** | Central metaphysis | Eccentric metaphysis | Eccentric epiphyseo-metaphyseal to subchondral bone |
| **Expansion** | Not wider than physis | Blow-out, wider than physis | Expanded, thin cortex |
| **Margin** | Sclerotic, well-defined | Thin eggshell rim | Non-sclerotic, geographic |
| **MRI** | Single fluid cavity | Multiple fluid-fluid levels | Solid, low T2 areas |
| **Genetics** | NFATC2 fusions (recent) | USP6 rearrangement | H3F3A G34W |
| **Key sign** | Fallen fragment | Fluid-fluid levels | Reaches subchondral bone |

## 6. Fibrous and other cystic-looking lesions (common distractors)
### Non-ossifying fibroma (NOF) and fibrous cortical defect
- **Commonest bone lesion in children** (fibrous cortical defects in about 30% of children); age 5-20; **"don't touch" lesion**.
- **Distal femur and distal or proximal tibia metaphysis**; **eccentric, cortically based, multiloculated lucency with a scalloped sclerotic margin**; long axis parallel to the bone; migrates away from the physis and **heals spontaneously by sclerosis** in adolescence.
- Histology: storiform fibroblasts, giant cells, haemosiderin and foam cells; **KRAS / FGFR1 (MAPK pathway)** mutations.
- **Fracture risk (Arata):** lesion involving **over 50% of the transverse diameter on AP and lateral views and over 33 mm long**.
- **Treatment:** observation; pathological fractures usually heal in a cast; curettage and grafting for large symptomatic lesions or after fracture with persistent risk.
- **Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome:** multiple NOFs + café-au-lait spots (+ learning difficulty, hypogonadism, ocular and cardiac anomalies); now considered part of **neurofibromatosis type 1** spectrum.

### Fibrous dysplasia (FD)
- **Activating GNAS mutation (Gs alpha, codon R201)**, post-zygotic somatic mosaic - **not inherited**; increased cAMP leads to immature fibro-osseous tissue.
- **Monostotic (about 70-80%):** **ribs (commonest), proximal femur, craniofacial bones**, tibia. **Polyostotic:** often unilateral, femur, tibia, pelvis.
- **McCune-Albright syndrome:** polyostotic FD + **café-au-lait spots with irregular "coast of Maine" borders** (NF1 spots have smooth "coast of California" borders) + **endocrinopathy** (**precocious puberty** commonest, especially girls; hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, Cushing syndrome) and **FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting (hypophosphataemic rickets/osteomalacia)**.
- **Mazabraud syndrome:** FD + **intramuscular myxomas**.
- **Radiograph:** **ground-glass** matrix, well-defined lesion with a **thick sclerotic "rind"**, expansion, endosteal scalloping; long lesion in the diaphysis/metaphysis; **shepherd's crook deformity** (coxa vara of the proximal femur); bowing; leg-length discrepancy.
- **Histology:** irregular curvilinear woven bone trabeculae (**"Chinese letters" / "alphabet soup"**) in fibrous stroma, **without osteoblastic rimming**.
- **Management:**
  - Observation for asymptomatic lesions; **bisphosphonates** (IV pamidronate/zoledronate) reduce pain (do not heal the lesion).
  - **Treat hypophosphataemia** and endocrine disease before surgery.
  - **Autogenous cancellous graft is resorbed and replaced by dysplastic bone**; use **cortical allograft struts** (resorb slowly) if grafting.
  - **Proximal femur / shepherd's crook:** **valgus osteotomy with intramedullary fixation (cephalomedullary nail)** - load-sharing intramedullary devices are preferred over plates in children and for long-term protection.
  - Malignant transformation (osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma) **under 1%**, higher in McCune-Albright and after **radiotherapy (avoid)**.

### Osteofibrous dysplasia (OFD, Campanacci lesion) and adamantinoma
| Feature | Osteofibrous dysplasia | Adamantinoma |
|---|---|---|
| **Age** | **Under 10 years** | 20-40 years |
| **Site** | **Anterior cortex of the tibial diaphysis** (also fibula); anterior bowing | **Anterior tibial diaphysis** (about 85-90% in the tibia) |
| **Radiograph** | Intracortical multiloculated lucencies with sclerosis | Multiloculated "soap-bubble" lytic lesion, may breach cortex, satellite lesions |
| **Histology** | Woven bone **with osteoblastic rimming** (unlike FD), scattered keratin-positive cells | **Epithelial (keratin-positive) nests** in fibro-osseous stroma |
| **Nature** | Benign; may regress after puberty | **Low-grade malignant**; late lung and node metastases (about 15-30%) |
| **Treatment** | **Observation**; bracing for bowing; delay surgery until after about age 15 (early resection recurs) | **Wide en bloc resection** with intercalary reconstruction (allograft, vascularised fibula, bone transport) or amputation; chemo- and radio-resistant |

- **OFD-like (differentiated) adamantinoma** is an intermediate entity; OFD and adamantinoma are thought to form a spectrum, so biopsy aggressive or enlarging OFD-like lesions.

### Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)
- Clonal proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells; **BRAF V600E mutation in about 50%**.
- **Age 5-15 (most under 30)**; **"great mimicker"** (of Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis).
- **Skull is the commonest site** (**punched-out lesion with bevelled edges**, "hole within a hole", button sequestrum), **vertebra plana** (thoracic spine, collapse with preserved discs; Calvé disease), ribs, pelvis, long bone diaphysis (may show periosteal reaction).
- **Histology:** Langerhans cells with **grooved "coffee-bean" nuclei**, eosinophils; **CD1a, CD207 (langerin) and S100 positive**; **Birbeck granules ("tennis racquet")** on electron microscopy.
- **Clinical forms:** unifocal bone (eosinophilic granuloma, commonest, best prognosis); **Hand-Schüller-Christian** (multifocal: **skull lesions, exophthalmos, diabetes insipidus**); **Letterer-Siwe** (disseminated multisystem disease under 2-3 years, poor prognosis).
- **Treatment:** skeletal survey/PET to assess spread; unifocal lesions often **heal spontaneously** - biopsy, then observation, **intralesional methylprednisolone**, or curettage; **vertebra plana**: observation ± brace (partial height restoration in children), surgery only for neurological deficit or instability; low-dose radiotherapy rarely; **multisystem disease: chemotherapy (vinblastine + prednisolone)**, BRAF inhibitors in refractory cases.

### Other lucent lesions
- **Brown tumour (osteitis fibrosa cystica):** hyperparathyroidism; multiple lytic lesions, subperiosteal resorption of the **radial side of middle phalanges**, salt-and-pepper skull; giant cells on histology mimic GCT; **resolve after parathyroidectomy**.
- **Intraosseous ganglion:** subchondral, adults, medial malleolus, around the knee and carpal bones; sclerotic rim; curettage if symptomatic.
- **Epidermoid inclusion cyst:** **distal phalanx** or skull after penetrating trauma; well-defined lytic lesion; curettage.
- **Intraosseous lipoma:** calcaneus (central calcification), proximal femur; observation.
- **Mnemonic for lucent lesions (FEGNOMASHIC):** Fibrous dysplasia, Enchondroma / Eosinophilic granuloma, GCT, NOF, Osteoblastoma, Metastasis / Myeloma, ABC, Simple bone cyst, Hyperparathyroidism (brown tumour), Infection, Chondroblastoma / Chondromyxoid fibroma. Lesions not likely over 30 years: EG, NOF, ABC, SBC, chondroblastoma; GCT needs a closed physis.
